summary:
Letters from the Left Behind is an interactive digital storybook that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each of five machines (the Apollo 11 lander, Voyager 1, Opportunity, Curiosity and Ingenuity) tells its own story in a first-person letter. Every chapter has an illustration, a short "science note" and a status badge showing whether the machine is still working, still traveling or has finished its mission.
The project addresses the challenge by turning hardware facts into a story children can follow. It shows what each machine was built to do, what it discovered, and where it is now. It matters because it helps young people see that space missions leave a lasting legacy, and it encourages them to keep telling these stories and to imagine the missions they might lead one day.
details:
What it does: Letters from the Left Behind is an interactive storybook for school-age space fans. Five NASA machines tell their own story in first-person letters: the Apollo 11 lander, Voyager 1, Opportunity, Curiosity and Ingenuity. Each chapter has an illustration, a short science note and a status badge showing whether the machine is still working, still traveling or has finished its mission. The last page shows where all five are now.
Benefits and impact: Children meet real NASA hardware and the science it made possible through a story instead of a fact sheet. Telling each story from the machine's point of view makes them easy to care about. It also shows young people that space missions leave a lasting legacy, and it invites them to tell the next story.
Tools used: HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the storybook, hand-drawn SVG illustrations, and PowerPoint and PDF for the demo. Facts come from NASA and JPL mission pages. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write and build the project, and we reviewed the content ourselves.
Creativity: The story is told by the machines themselves, as letters, and links the Moon, Mars and deep space in time order.
Factors considered: Age-appropriate language, scientific accuracy, a mix of machines that are still working, finished or still traveling, and a layout that works on phones.
